source.title: Local Linearity and Double Descent in Catastrophic Overfitting

record.file_problem: None noted; the full two-page paper is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests epoch-wise double descent in the new setting of adversarial training, using test robustness over training epochs.
record.gate_note: The authors report qualitative epoch-wise robustness trends in Figures 1–4 and describe which settings recover after a decline. The cited double-descent results from prior work are not this study's results. Local-linearity and orthogonality findings that do not report the claim's test-robustness trajectory are not separate rows.
record.test_reason: The authors track adversarial test robustness over training epochs under FGSM adversarial training. They describe a decline followed by recovery that they call double descent, which bears on V2 in a new setting. The evidence is qualitative and figure-only, with no numbers and no check against an interpolation threshold.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that high local linearity is likely sufficient but not necessary to prevent catastrophic overfitting, and may induce orthogonal weights. They also say they identify double descent during adversarial training when local linearity is not controlled (no regularization and orthogonal regularization). They call for formal investigation of this double descent.
record.recipe_differences: Uses FGSM adversarial training and tracks adversarial test robustness on a small CNN; it does not reproduce the original study's broader double-descent sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported epoch-wise robustness pattern differs by regularization setting: double descent is described without regularization and with orthogonal regularization, while robustness does not decline with GradAlign, alone or combined with orthogonal regularization.
record.problems: The study uses a 5-layer CNN and 1,000 test samples; the authors note that computational constraints prevented use of ResNet-18 and replication of larger-network performance. The double-descent evidence is qualitative in figures, with no numerical values or uncertainty estimates stated in the text.

untested.parts: No model-size sweep; a single 5-layer CNN.
Ordinary (clean) test error over epochs is not reported in the text. There is no link to an interpolation threshold or to label noise, and no quantitative values.
No capacity sweep or other model classes.
No label-noise manipulation, no multiple peaks, and no tuned regularization strength.

missing.what: Whether clean (standard) test accuracy over epochs, which Figures 1–4 may show, also follows a fall-rise-fall shape; the text does not say.

record.verdict_notes: Two-page workshop-style paper. The double-descent evidence is a qualitative recovery after catastrophic overfitting in adversarial robustness. This may be a different mechanism from epoch-wise double descent as defined in the original sources: there is no interpolation threshold or noise analysis. Only 1,000 test samples are used, and no uncertainty is reported. The label 'challenges' in the record for r3 and r4 is replaced by 'limits_scope': V2 does not require the effect under every regularizer.

versions.untested_parts: Tests adversarial test robustness over epochs, not ordinary test error; no model-size or sample-size sweep.
No training-sample-size comparison near an interpolation threshold.
No comparison across model classes or capacity sweep past an interpolation point.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested against peak locations.
Does not test label-noise or variance as the peak's cause, multiple peaks, or disappearance under optimally tuned regularization.
Does not recount complexity using an effective number of parameters.
